utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted by Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. The Defence teams, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Today on behalf of Mr. Kubura, Mr. Rodney Dixon assisted by Nermin Mulalic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, the interpreters have a problem in the French booth with the air-conditioning and it's very difficult for them to work like that. We are now going to resume the testimony of the expert witness and I am going to give the floor to Mr. Bourgon for his additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Bourgon: [In English]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. General, further to the cross-examination conducted by my colleague yesterday, there are a few issues I would like to confirm with you. Now, I am sure that my colleague from the Prosecution did not intend to confuse you with his questions yesterday, as he mentioned to you. Nonetheless, I don't think my colleague was successful in avoiding to confuse you and this is why I would like to clarify a few things that were mentioned yesterday. And my first question is very simple, and it goes as follows: What kind of questions did you expect from the Prosecution yesterday and were you surprised by the kind of questions that were asked of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised by the questions. I didn't expect those questions. I expected different questions, questions that would have to do more with the essence of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, there might be a reason for the kind of questions that you were asked. And even though the Prosecution did not challenge you directly, with respect to the validity of your report, as I believe he should have done, it is implicit from the questions that were put to you that the Prosecution is challenging the way and the manner in which you drafted your report. Did you understand that yesterday from the questions that were put to you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large extent I did and I assumed that this was their objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I would like to do this morning, General, is to ask you some additional questions on the methodology or, to use the words of my colleague from the Prosecution, the means by which you produced your report. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I would simply ask you this morning, General, is to concentrate on my questions and, if you have any doubt as to any of the meaning of my questions, please don't hesitate to interrupt me or to tell me and I will try to the best of my ability to clarify the question. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, yesterday, in response to a question from my colleague from the Prosecution, you mentioned that you retired officially from the Army of the Federation on 31 August of 2004, and you also said that you agreed to take on the challenge of drafting this report in May of 2004 or sometime in early June. Do you recall giving this answer?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, last week, in response to my question, which was on the 21st of March, you said about the same thing. Now, that was on page 43, lines 7 to 17 of the transcript. And you mentioned that you had retired on 31 August 2004 and that you started working on the report while you were still in the military. Do you remember giving me that answer on the 21st of March?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question, General, is the fact that you were still in the army when you agreed to draft a report and that you started to draft a report, did this have any influence on the manner in which you drafted the report or the conclusions that you reached?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me whether the fact that I was still in the army had any influence on the manner in which I drafted the report and the conclusions that I arrived at; is that your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct, General. Did this -- does this fact, that you were still a serving member of the Army of the Federation, did this fact have any influence on either the manner in which you did the work or the conclusions that you reached?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of June last year, I underwent surgery of my thyroid gland in the clinical centre in Sarajevo. I was removed from certain activities connected with this job for 15 days. After that I was on sick leave and I never returned to work in the BiH army until the moment I was retired. Before the surgery, I had some preparations for this surgery, and in fact and formally my engagement in the Army of the Federation stopped at the beginning of June last year. Legally and because of the procedure, because of the manner the decisions are made, I was formally retired on the 31st of August last year or, in other words, on the 1st of September last year. I knew about all of that and in formal terms my engagement in the army did not have any influence on my work on this task, the task of preparing this expert report, because I was not present in the army at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now the fact that you were still a member serving in the Army of the Federation, if we take into consideration that General Hadzihasanovic is a former member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did this have any influence or did you feel any pressure to draft your report in one way or another because you were a member of the same army as General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a serious person and I know very well what the meaning of the Tribunal in The Hague is and what its overall significance is. I know the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina very well. I know the situation as it was during the last war, and not for a moment I would dream of playing with a certain peoples' destinies. I would never embark on something that would be dishonest and immoral. Whatever you mentioned in your question would seem to me to be immoral and dishonest and those things are the things I never allowed myself to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now in response to one of my questions also on the 21st of March, and the reference is the same - that is the transcript on page 43, lines 7 to 17 - you mentioned that after you retired from the military, you got more involved in drafting the report. And my question is, when did you do most of the work? Before or after your retirement from the army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the work and the key parts of that work were done after my retirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday the Prosecution asked you if, when you accepted to draft this report, you had any doubt as to the innocence of the two accused. Now, that was yesterday and this was on page 19, lines 5 to 9. Then, at my request, the question was repeated. And that was on page 21, lines 1 and 2. But this time you were asked whether you had any beliefs as to the guilt or the innocence of the two accused. Now, initially your answer was that you were even more confused by the second question than by the first. An then, at page 21, lines 5 to 7, you said the following, and I quote: "I was informed of the main elements and facts of the indictment; however, I did not give myself the right, nor did anybody ask me to do that. Nobody ever instructed me as to whether I should form an opinion of their responsibility." Now, my question, General, is: Should we understand, from your answer, that you had no opinion one way or another when you agreed to draft the report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would more or less be the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution went on to ask you if you had read the indictment, and your response was "yes". This is at page 21, lines 17 to 23. My question is, would it have been possible for you to answer question 7 in your report without reading the indictment? And maybe you want to look at question 7 - which was put to you by the Defence - in your report to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Question number 7, paragraph 18, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at, in your report, in the first part where you have paragraph 18, and then inside the block you have question 7. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is, would it have been possible for you to answer this question without reading the indictment?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my next question relates to what -- to your response to a question by the Prosecution, and this was on page 19, at lines 15 to 21, yesterday. Now, I just need to find the right quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President, I had the transcript. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, General, this was on page 19 and this was at line 15 to 21. And you said here: "I don't know, to this very day, whether these two are guilty or not. I'm just trying to show you, through the documents, and to explain to the Trial Chamber the military steps and the military actions, the actions and steps of a commander in the given circumstances that prevailed at the time. I'm trying to explain why things were done in a certain way and not in another way, whether things should have been done Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in that particular way and how things were being done at that time." Now my question to you, General, is, in terms of what you were asked to do in drafting the report, were you asked to give your opinion as to General Hadzihasanovic was innocent or guilty, or were you asked to asked to give your opinion as to whether General Hadzihasanovic fulfilled his duty as commander of the 3rd Corps in the circumstances ruling at the time and from the perspective of a senior military commander? Which of the two was it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to offend anybody, but I would like to say that the first part of your question is rather ridiculous. It would have been preposterous for me to say and nobody asked for me to do that, to say whether General Hadzihasanovic and Brigadier Kubura are innocent or guilt guilty. Nobody ever asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were you attempting to do when you drafted this report? What was it that you were asked to do as a military expert at the command level or at the level of senior commanders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the questions that I was asked to study, all the documents available to me, to provide answers in the most precise and clear manner. And whenever the questions called for that, I was asked to give my opinion about the steps that were taken by the two commanders, what those steps were like in the situation that prevailed. And when looking at those steps, from a military angle, were these steps justified or unjustified, and to what extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I move to a different topic. In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that the military expert initially retained by the Defence was Sead Delic. Can you inform the Trial Chamber as to who is Sead Delic and, if you know, what position did he occupy during the war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sead Delic is a general major, I believe that that was his rank, when he was retired, and he retired even before me. I believe that he retired two years before me, if not more. He hails from eastern Bosnia. He was also an officer of the JNA up to the beginning of the war, just like me. He served in places different to me. I believe that he was in Croatia when the war started, and that he held one of the military positions in Varazdin which is in the northern part of Croatia, when JNA units withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia in the course of 1991, just like I arrived in Zenica, I believe that he was wounded and he was transported to Belgrade, to the military medical centre for rehabilitation. After that he arrived in Tuzla. I don't know how he found himself there, but he did come to Tuzla. And when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an internationally recognised state, he joined the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina. He's my senior by a few years, two, three or four years, I don't know exactly. He performed rather important duties in the JNA and he held very high positions in the JNA. In the BiH army, at the beginning, he was the commander of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Tuzla. And during that short period of time, he was my subordinate until the moment I was captured, because at the time I was the commander of the district staff of the Tuzla Territorial Defence. After that he became the commander of the OG and then he became the commander of the 2nd Corps of the BiH army in Tuzla. And I believe that he held that position in the Federation Army until the moment he was retired. So he remained the commander of the 2nd Corps. Currently he is involved in politics and he is a member of parliament in the parliament of either the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I can't be sure of that. He holds a master of arts degree in political sciences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, did General Sead Delic try to influence you, one way or another, with respect to the drafting of your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that he didn't try to influence me, he couldn't influence me. I wouldn't want to say anything else because I'm on different terms with Sead Delic and that has been the case since the beginning of the war. So if I may put it this way, our relationship is purely official, but this has nothing to do with this case. But he didn't try to influence me in the way that you suggested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General, yesterday, in response to a question by the Prosecution, you mentioned receiving some material which was drafted by Sead Delic before you took over from him. And my question is: Were you influenced, in one way or another, by whatever material was given to you by Sead Delic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to refer you to paragraph 10 of your report. Now, this is in the first part where you say that you requested to meet with Sead Delic. To use the exact words in your report, it says "I expressed my interest, provided my curriculum vitae and requested to meet with the former military expert retained by the Defence before confirming my ability." Now, in paragraph 11, you go on to say: Having obtained a better understanding of the work required, I agreed to take on the challenge. Or to use the exact word, "I was ready to take on this challenge." My question is, was the purpose of meeting with Sead Delic to obtain such a better understanding of the work required to produce an expert report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I saw Sead Delic once or twice and I don't consider those times when I saw him to be meetings. We didn't discuss the subjects. When we saw each other, it was only for a few minutes. Later I asked him over the phone for his book. I think I mentioned that yesterday, because his book clarifies and explains the role of all international bodies, from UNPROFOR, IFOR, SFOR, the OSC, the UNHCR, to a lot of international bodies in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the course of the war. And at one point in time, in one of the first versions, there was a question or subquestion about the role of the international bodies in the Central Bosnian area in 1993. But later on this question was deleted. I was provided with his book, but I never used it. And that is all the contact we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I now move to a different issue, and I would ask that you look at paragraph 13 of your report. I will quote this paragraph for you and it says here: "I was given a copy of the material available at that time and I was informed that additional documents would be given to me as they became available. I was also told that I could call upon the team investigator to locate additional material, if required." General, can you give us the name of the team investigator you are referring to in paragraph 13 of your report.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already mentioned this on a number of occasions. His name was General Mustafa Polutak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now yesterday, and this is at page 28, line 25, and also page 29 lines 1 to 3, and I will quote what you said then. You were asked whether you knew that Mustafa Polutak was the investigator of the Defence. And then you went on to say -- and I'm looking for the exact place in the transcript. Yes, sorry. I gave you the wrong quote. It's page 28, line 25. I was looking at page 25. Sorry. Now I found it. Page 28, line 25 and page 29, lines 1 to 3. The question put to you was: "And General Mustafa Polutak was or is an investigator working for the Defence team of General Hadzihasanovic, is that correct." And your answer was: "I can't confirm that. I had contact with him, but as to what he does, I don't know. I assume that is the case." Was there ever any doubt in your mind as to the fact that Mustafa Polutak was an investigator for the Defence team of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really want to provide you with precise answers but that creates certain problems and confusion. I said that I'm not sure that Brigadier Kubura was the brigade commander up until the 6th of August, 1993 because there is not a single order, there's not a single document about this. I can't confirm that then. We know what would be used as a confirmation of certain claims. I didn't see any documents or orders from this Tribunal related to General Mustafa Polutak in which it was stated that he was what he was. It wasn't anyone's duty to show me such documents, but everything that I did was done with General Mustafa Polutak and I could see that he had direct contact with you, and with Mrs. Residovic, and with others. And I saw that he had free access to the archives when he needed something and the Federation Army, for example, and he had contact with Mrs. Mirna, I don't know her last name, Milanovic -- or Mirkovic, I think that was her surname. As to everything else that I mentioned, as to all the other people that I mentioned, I didn't consider them to be particularly important. The conversations I had with those people are completely official. They lasted from a minute or half a minute up until half an hour. Ten or fifteen minutes. And when I had to draw maps, I asked others where the line was around Travnik or where the defence line was around Bugojno or I asked about certain dates that appeared in documents. I asked them about various dates in order to obtain confirmation, et cetera, et cetera. Then I failed to mention my wife, for example, who brought me a book from a -- or who brought me books from the library because she -- because she works in a library and she brought me all the books I needed to read and prepare for this expert report, that, what is the objective of this question, that's what I'm asking myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will move on to a different topic and we will have the chance to discuss a little further the people that you had conversations with, because this was an issue raised by my colleague. But I now would like to go back to paragraph 13 of your report where it says, in the first sentence: "I was given a copy of the material available at that time and I was informed that additional documents would be given to me as they became available." So my question is, were you in fact given this material as you say and what was that material you were given at that time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll probably have to provide you with the same answer that I provided yesterday. Reference was made to additional material. I'm not sure what the importance of this material was. I received certain material from General Polutak. I read through the material. Were the summary -- the reports from certain number of witnesses or not, I don't know. Perhaps they were. But this was never clarified. Although this material had been described as additional reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, in paragraph 13, I go back to the sentence I referred to a little earlier where it says "I was told that I could call upon the team investigator to locate additional material". Now, I would like to refer you to page 40 of the transcript yesterday, at lines 5 to 16 and to quote what you said then. And the question was as follows: "Can you elaborate upon that answer that you gave? What did you mean by using documents from the archives of the Federation Army?" And your answer was: "Let me give you an example. I wanted, on two or three occasions, to look at the zones of responsibility of various corps and how they changed over time and this could not be found on any of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the existing maps. Then I asked for some topographic maps from the archives of the BiH army and I did that through General Polutak. I consulted these topographic maps and, after that, I used the information that I obtained from those topographic maps in order to compile my annexes." And then the question, the following question was: "Sir, other than topographic maps, did you make any request for documents from archives of the ABiH or from any other Bosnian government archives?" And your response was: "I did not request any particular documents. Mustafa Polutak was the one who had the list of documents that were registered with the Tribunal. I did not find it necessary." Now my question to you, General, is, those dealings you had with Mustafa Polutak, as you say, on two or three occasions, to get topographic maps, is this what you were referring to when you said that you could have access to Mustafa Polutak to get further material?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try to make the question -- or to clarify the question. In paragraph 13 of your report, you say "I was told that I could call upon the team investigator" - now we know that this is Mustafa Polutak - "to locate additional material." In your response to a question from the Prosecution yesterday, you said that on two or three occasions, you asked Mustafa Polutak for topographic maps. Can we link your response yesterday to what you were told you could do while preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I refer you now to paragraph 15 of your report and it says, in the first sentence that "During the period from 1 June to 17 December, I was provided with additional material on a regular basis." My question is very simple: This additional material, did it include documents, witness summaries, or both?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will clarify the question. You mentioned in paragraph 15 that you were provided with additional material on a regular basis. What was this material? What was this additional material?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material referred to wasn't additional material, but the material that's behind me, that is all the material that -- initially I started using the first binder, and then the second binder. So the second binder was the additional material, and then the third binder was additional material, et cetera. That's what I meant when I said "additional." Initially I must admit that I didn't think there was so much material. However when I started working on the report, then after a certain period of time, I realised that the material I had to read was extremely voluminous and that's what I meant when I said "additional." And finally, I realised that there was all this material that is contained in the binders behind me, if you're referring to additional material that is not included in these binders, well then that's a mistake. That's not what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to move to paragraph 21 of your report, which deals with what you have just mentioned. I would like you to take a few seconds to read what you wrote in paragraph 21 of your report. Now, my question, General, is the following: Is this the material on which you based your opinion in your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the material behind me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring, General, to the material which is described in paragraph 21. Is this what you used, as you mentioned here, to prepare your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the material used, but in order to avoid any confusion I was trying to be a little clearer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it included in the binders that you have beside you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I can't claim for sure that perhaps a document appeared or arrived was contained in the binders for sure. But, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in those materials that were given to you, did you see any documents having a number preceded by the letter "P," some documents preceded by the letters "DH" for "delta hotel," and some documents with a number preceded by the letters "DK," or "delta kilo," and some documents with a number but without any letters? Do you recall seeing such documents and can you explain what these documents are?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw many such documents, all of the documents here are of that kind. But the Defence has one way in which the documents are marked. Other documents are marked in a different way. Documents are marked in different ways for General Hadzihasanovic and for Brigadier Kubura and the Prosecution documents, yet again, marked in another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall, General, seeing documents with a number but without any letters? And do you recall what these documents were?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a lot of documents of that kind, with such numbers, five or six numbers. And I don't really know what kind of documents they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now yesterday, General, there seemed to be some confusion with regards to paragraph 21 of your reports, and that was on page 37 at lines 4 to 9 of the transcript. And the confusion seemed to be in the words "I have also relied on proposed exhibits by the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic, and the Defence for Brigadier Kubura." These documents, are they included in your binders behind you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly I don't believe that that is the word I used. I don't believe I said that I relied on proposed documents, on proposed exhibits. I don't know how that was interpreted, but I wouldn't comment on that. As far as these proposed exhibits are concerned, I've already provided you with an answer. All I can do is repeat my answer. If you're referring to the documents that we've described as additional documents -- what do you mean by proposed documents?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is just the purpose of my question, General. It's just to clarify, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and I'm referring to paragraph 21 of your report. Now maybe it's the language that is different between the English version and the original. But at the end of this paragraph, you say, at least from the English version, "in addition, I have also relied on proposed exhibits by the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic and the Defence for Brigadier Amir Kubura." And then you say, "when referring to the exhibits, I used the numbers provided to me by the Defence." Now, I would simply like to know whether these proposed exhibits are documents that were given to you and that are included in your binders.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General can you say this answer again, because the transcript -- sorry. Now I have the transcript. Sorry, General. Thank you. Now, I would like to go back to a question which I asked you on the 21st of March, and that was on page 45 at lines 1 to 4, where you mentioned that for each binder there was a list of documents. Do you recall saying this and showing to the Trial Chamber one of those binders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I take all of your binders, and I take the sum of all of the lists at the beginning of each binder, would that make up all the documents that you used for your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have such a compiled list anywhere? Or you worked separately for each binder and never collected these documents or these lists together?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the list that I had was comprehensive or not, but I had a list in Sarajevo. I don't have it on me. I don't have it among the documents that are either in the hotel or in my briefcase, that I have on me today. In any case, I don't have that list on me today here in the courtroom. And the one that I had in Sarajevo, I don't know whether it was comprehensive or not. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If need be, we'll go back to trying to locate. But my question is: Is there such a consolidated list of all the documents?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question, General, is: Were you ever instructed, by anyone, to look at different documents or to consult with people, other than what is in paragraph 21, to prepare your report? Were you ever instructed by the Defence to, say, Go and see more people, or, Look at other documents than this, what is in your binders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both cases, the answer is "no." Whatever I did and whoever I consulted with was my own doing and it had nothing whatsoever to do with the Defence team. I'm sure that you didn't even know about my contacts with anybody else until yesterday when I mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to move on to a different issue, General, and that is the question of witness summaries. But before I ask you a question specifically on the summaries themselves, I would like to know if you were or if you recall being given a CD Rom or maybe more than one CD Rom with all the transcripts of the witnesses, or of witnesses who appeared in this case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was given five CDs with a lot of material. A lot of that material was on those CDs that I studied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these CD Roms that you mention, are you talking about documents or transcripts? A transcript is where -- it looks like something you have on your screen. Were you given a CD Rom with something that looks like what you have on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents, documents. For the most part, the things that I studied, were documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now yesterday General you said that you had read the testimony of General Reinhardt - and we'll come back to that - and you mentioned that there were two binders and five days and you provided a lot of information. But on those CDs, was there any similar transcript to what you read from General Reinhardt? If you know.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe yes. Maybe no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now General, the -- in response to a question by my colleague yesterday, you mentioned that the witness summaries were given to you in Sarajevo. Do you remember what the purpose of these summaries was? Or why they were given to you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the purpose was for me to study those summaries, to study those testimonies, and to get acquainted with what these people said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General, do you recall being given additional summaries while you arrived here in The Hague no later than last weekend while you were preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. In my briefcase I have General Reinhardt's report. Not the transcript, but his report, which I studied thoroughly, which I read two or three times. I made my notes on it. And I believe that I have two groups of summaries of that sort in my briefcase, the summaries of various witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these summaries that you have in your briefcase, these were given to you quite recently, after you handed in your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday, in response to a question by my colleague, you said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that those summaries were in your own language. And my question is: Do you remember receiving some of those summaries also in English?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, when I looked at them, one group of summaries is in English, and the other is in Bosnian. I'm referring to the material that I had in the hotel, and some of it I have in my briefcase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This material that you have that you looked at, could you use it to produce your report? Or did you use that when you drafted the report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this material maybe ten or fifteen days ago, some 15 days ago or so. And before that there was another set of summaries that I received 10 or 15 days before that. So objectively speaking, there was no way for me to use any of them in drafting my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you also recall, General, having received such summaries? And yesterday you referred to a -- I think you said something like 150, or it may be 160 pages that you mentioned. Do you recall having received those summaries before you wrote your report and having used these summaries in drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness said there was 100 to 150 pages. That's on page 27 -- pages 26 and 27 from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have all the quotes, almost all the quotes. This particular one I don't have, so I may have been mistaken on the number. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, yesterday you said anywhere from 100 to 150 pages, but the number of pages, to me, is not the purpose of my question. My question is, rather, whether you read witness summaries in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read them subsequently, after I handed over -- or maybe there was a bit of an overlap in time, but most of them I read after I had handed over my expert report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these summaries, General, were they useful in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not particularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go to paragraph 21 of your report. Sorry, let me go first to paragraph 14 and 15 of your report. In these paragraphs, you mention a cut-off date and there and to be some confusion as to what the cut-off date was or what is a cut-off date. Now, again I don't know if it's the translation, and if you have something different in the original report. But you also come back, at paragraph 21 and you mention not the word "cut-off date," but you again mention the date of 17 December. And my understanding was that this report was based on everything that you received until 17 December as well as the witness summaries who had appeared, but no later than 17 December. Is that -- is that what you wanted to say in paragraphs 14, 15 and 21? I just want you to explain to the Trial Chamber what exactly you meant by these paragraphs and what you meant by the word "cut-off date." And is there a difference between the material that you used in drafting the report and the material that you were given after, that you looked subsequently, as you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any difference here. This is more or less the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it would be important here, General, for you to explain whether you received any documents after you received -- after handing in your report - and the date you gave it to the Defence or to us was on the 22nd of February - if you received documents after this date, and of course that you could not use when you drafted the report. I think you did confirm this, but I would like to hear it from you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when I received the second set of summaries, of the summaries of witness testimonies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only have two more questions with respect to this issue. My first question is: All of these witness summaries that you received, did you ever have any problems with the summaries, in terms of there was not enough information, or the information was too vague? Or did you ask for any clarification with respect to the summaries that you received?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of those summaries, General, would it be impossible for you to put them altogether and to hand them to the Trial Chamber if that was necessary?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can provide the Trial Chamber at this very moment with what I have on me, now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you have on you now, is that all the summaries? Or are there other summaries? Is that all the summaries you were given?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have all of them, but I can't say that for a fact. I can't be 100 per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I move on to a different issue, General, and I see we only have ten minutes before the break -- sorry I have one more question on this issue, and that is: On the basis of those, of the material you received, after you gave the Defence your report, did you see a need, on the basis of the documents or the witness summaries, to modify any of your conclusions in the report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to move to the issue of the persons with whom you had various conversation. And in response to a question earlier, you said that these conversations took place on your own initiative. Now, what I would like to know is whether any of these persons - and we could go back to the transcript, but I don't think it is necessary - whether any of these persons tried to influence you, one way or another, with respect to the contents of your report.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody influenced me. Nobody even tried to influence me. But the main thing is that they could not influence me, because, in my contacts with these people, a lot of them didn't even know, were not even aware why I was talking to them. Only a few of them knew that I was talking to them because of the expert report that I was preparing. The majority of them, they didn't know, because our conversations were absolutely informal, and none of these conversations lasted more than five or six minutes. The only exception being Remzija Siljaic on who I spoke with to or three occasions and each of these occasions our conversations lasted about ten minutes. And not for a single moment did I find these contacts important in any sense. And these people did not have any influence on me whatsoever. And the same goes for the people who helped me in technical terms, in drafting my report. Those people were my typist, the lady who typed my report and that's how she helped me. She is a high school graduate. There was also this lad who drew some ten or fifteen topographic maps for me; he also is a high school graduate. Also there was this lad who helped me with the computer; he has just graduated from the university. These people were my technical personnel. When it comes to the professional expert part of my report, I am the only one responsible for the drafting of this report. And as I told you yesterday, I worked on my own, in my house, I have my computer there. I had the Internet connection there. I have my e-mail connection there, and everything else that I used. I did spend a certain time in Mrs. Residovic's office reading the vast amount of documents, and that is the long and the short of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I understand that it is not pleasant to be questioned after drafting a report and working so many months. And it is just that the Prosecution's challenge make it that I must ask you these questions and I hope you understand that. My next question to you is: At page 40, lines 24 and 25, as well as page 41, lines 1 to 4, you explain - and I will quote the exact words just to be sure - "and my answer was there isn't. On some occasions I double-checked with some other persons. I received the same answer and I was able to close the door on such a particular question. I did not need to look any further. I had my answer." And then you go on, because the Prosecution put a question to you: When you say that you double-checked information with other persons, can you tell us if you recall the identity of these persons and where they were employed. Then you go on to explain that these people were retired a long time ago and you provide some names. Now my question is simply, when you say that your conversations with those people were to double-check information, was that the purpose of these conversations? Or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first thing that you mentioned. I was checking myself. I sought confirmation for my beliefs, for what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the time has come for our first break. I will continue after the break. I don't know for how long, but I believe that I will need only half an hour to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is half past ten. We will resume at around five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Welcome back, General. Before I move on to my next question, I was looking at my notes during the break and I see that I missed one question that I should have been asking you, and that is: How many hours were you supposed to spend to draft this report or, to be more precise, for how many hours of work will you be paid to produce this report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did everything myself, in the sense that I acted as my own typist, at least for part of the report. I made the annexes myself on a computer and I, in fact, drew my own maps, my own topographic maps, and then I gave this young man, who was assisting me, to redraw these maps because he was technically quite capable. Later, I had to scan those topographic maps and that involves a lot of work. It was necessary to do this to be able to display how this was done on the computer. The process is very complex. Had I done all of this on my own, it would have been difficult and I -- it is very difficult for me to say how many hours I spent working on this. I know that, on average, I worked between five and ten hours a day, if not more. But to be quite frank, occasionally there were interruptions because I had other duties. If you calculate the total number of hours, well the total number of hours would be very high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, I will say my question again, because maybe I wasn't clear enough. I just wanted to ask you when you agreed to take on this challenge of drafting this report, were you told that you would be paid a certain amount of money, and that was based on the number of hours you were supposed to spend working on this report? What I'm interested in is, if that is the case, how many hours were you supposed to work on this report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that I should spend 80 working hours, that was for the initial version. And later, the number of hours was increased. But the actual number of hours that I spent working on this report is far greater. I'm not saying this with something particular in mind, but I just wanted to tell you what the situation actually was. I spent two or three times many hours on the project.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to move on to the issue of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. separation of the documents. In response to a question by the Prosecution yesterday, you said that you separated the documents yourself. And I believe - now I don't have the exact citation here, but maybe my colleague can correct me if I don't use the exact words - but you said that you separated the documents by a number of themes. Do you have a list of those themes that you used?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I separated the documents, placed them in different categories, on the basis of the questions or rather the themes. I did that myself. As for the other questions, as for the other part of the question when I said that I separated or singled out some documents, I did that and created a certain list of some documents that I thought were very important or had to do with important periods of time or had to do with certain territories. Yesterday I mentioned an example. I separated a certain number of documents about direct and open cooperation between the Republika Srpska army and the Croatian Defence Council. I thought that this might be necessary given all the questions I would be asked when my report was being discussed. I thought it would be good to have these documents within my reach. So that is why I created certain categories of documents, on the basis of questions that I believed to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, yesterday you were asked by the Prosecution to pull out a document, and I must admit I was quite impressed with the speed with which you pulled out this document. Can you explain what the methodology you used to be able to pick this document so quickly in response to the question by my colleague. I'm referring to the document related to, I guess it was the appointment of Brigadier Kubura as Chief of Staff and deputy commander. How did you go about pulling this document so quick from all of your binders there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple. When all of these documents behind me were prepared, I tried to categorize them on the basis of the type of document, or rather on the basis of the units concerned. Finally in terms of the type of document and then the units and all the documents had to be in chronological order. So if I was asked yesterday whether there was such-and-such a document, such-and-such an order, first I asked myself where I might find that document, since the document concerned was an order and the document concerned the 7th Muslim brigade alone, it had nothing to do with any other units or with any other areas, and as a result I came to the conclusion that it might be in the certain binder, binder marked the 7th Muslim brigade. I took that binder and all the documents in all the binders being arranged in chronological order, I found the document on the basis of its date. That's why I was able to find it so quickly. But there are a certain number of documents here which were copied, so it's possible that some -- that there are several copies of some documents contained in various places in these binders because the document concerns a number of units or a number of areas, a number of activities, et cetera. So these documents have been copied and they're in each of these binders. For example, if I had been asked for a document that had to do with measures taken, since I have a number of binders, five or six binders that concern measures that were taken, I would then have a look at the date again, and the terms of time are quite clearly marked on the binders, on the binders that relate to measures, so I would immediately see the period of time that the document related to. I would then find the date of the binder and I would like for that document in that binder and I would find it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, I'm not sure if you do have a list, but in case you don't have a list, I would ask the assistance of the usher to maybe give you the microphone that you can hold in your hand and I would ask that you read the title of each of your binders that you have in the back so that we have this for the record in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please? What do you want me to do exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you can just read and explain what you find in each of these binders that you prepared. Maybe the title is enough. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I take the binders off this support or should I just do it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in this manner? The first binder says: "Looting, destruction of buildings," religious buildings. All the documents that have to do with this subject have been placed in this binder. The next binder is this one, marked "legal framework," binder number 2. It refers to the date from May 1993 to 2003. All documents, all the documents that have to do with legal matters are contained in this binder. The next binder is also number 1, the previous one was number 2. Number 1 is also marked "legal framework," and the date is up to May 1993. It wasn't possible to place all the documents in two binders. That's why they were placed in two binders [as interpreted]. The next two binders are numbered 1 and 2, marked the Croatian Defence Council. 1991 to 1992 is the period for the first binder and up to March 1993. Reference is made to 1991 and 1992 and up to March 1993. Binder number 2 says from April 1993 to the year 2002. All the documents that say anything about the HVO are contained in these two binders. In the second row below there is a binder marked, in capital letters: "DK," and the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. All the documents that directly relate to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade are contained in this binder. The next binder is marked "Dusina" and "Bugojno". All the documents that relate to the events in Dusina and in Bugojno have been placed in this binder. The next binder is marked "the music school," Mehurici, the village of Mehurici, "the Travnik barracks," the Sretno Hotel in Kakanj and the Serbian army, the Republika Srpska army. Documents that relate to those events have been placed in this binder. The next binder, and the following four binders or rather a total of five binders here are binders marked "miscellaneous". These binders contain documents that cannot be placed in any of the other binders, since they don't belong there. They should be placed in the binders marked "miscellaneous." The dates of these binders are from 1969 up until May 1993. The second binder from May 1993 up until August 1993. The third binder from August 1993 to January 1994. The fourth binder from 1994 to 2002. The fifth binder contains transcripts and final reports from expert commission of the UN and copies of certain rules and regulations. And in the bottom row there are binders. On the left there is a total of six binders. All six binders are marked "measures." Any documents that relate to measures taken by various bodies at various levels during that period of time in the ABiH and outside of the ABiH, all such documents which can't be placed in any of the other binders are contained in these six binders. The first binder has the date 1991 to February 1993. The second binder, February 1993 to May 1993. The third binder, from May 1993 to January 1993. The third binder, January 1993 to July 1993. The fifth binder, from July 1993 to November 1993. And the 6th binder, from November 1993 to the year 2001. And finally, there are two other binders, one marked "the village of Miletici," "the village of Maline," and "the village of Orasac." All the documents that relate to these three villages and the events in those villages have been placed in these -- in this binder. Then we have the last binder marked "the Mujahedin." All the documents that directly relate to the Mujahedin are in this binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, now yesterday you were asked a question by the Prosecution, and this was at 16 hours 27 minutes, and the question was: "Did you read all of these exhibits, described in paragraph 21, or did you review them and only read those which you believed were most important?" And your answer was: "My answer would be "yes." I read most of it. I read two-thirds of it. Some of the things I just reviewed, I skimmed through, as I believe that this was not important. But I can't tell you exactly how much of that material I only reviewed. It's impossible". Now, that was yesterday. On the 21st of March, I asked the exact same question. And your response then was, and this was at page 45, lines 12 to 18, where you said that there were over 5.000 documents, according to your count, that you did not read all of them because it was impossible, that you read the vast majority of the documents, and that the ones that you had not read, you at least had a look at. So can you just be -- again for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, did you physically handle every piece of paper by reading the vast majority and having a glance through the others? Or are there any documents that you never looked at?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as far as the 5.000 documents are concerned, I think that there was a mistake there or a slip. There are probably 5.000 pages, not 5.000 documents. In both cases, when I provided my answer, now that you have quoted my answers, I don't see any significant difference between my two answers. But I can repeat that I read the vast majority of all of these documents, and I don't believe that there are any documents that I didn't at least have a look at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I now move to another issue, which is that of the Internet. Now, this was a question put to you by the Prosecution yesterday, and this was at page 32, lines 7 to 25, where you mention having looked on the Internet, the proceedings in the trial of Sefer Halilovic, that you had also downloaded some media articles and also some documents about the proceedings. Now, at page 34, lines 23 to 25, here's what you said. "In very simple terms, I log on, and whatever happens I follow it. I just come across things that are on-line at the time and I read things. I listen to things. That's what I do." Now my question, General, is: This material from the Internet, does it have any bearing or did it have any bearing on the drafting of your report? Or is that something completely different?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back to the issue of the persons you spoke to. Yesterday, in response to a question by the Prosecution - and that was at 16 hours 49 minutes - you mention "The people I spoke to are wartime associates of mine from the ABiH 1st Corps, from the General Staff of the ABiH, and to a certain extent I spoke perhaps to some people who were from the ABiH 3rd Corps. I did not speak to anyone who was not a member of those bodies". Now, General, this may give the impression that you only spoke to people of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that there is a big scam here for you to produce a report that is on behalf of the army or that is one-sided or that was biased from all of these people who are only from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you reassure the Trial Chamber in this respect.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have drafted my report without contacting anyone, without discussing anything with anyone. I'm 100 per cent persuaded that the quality of the report would be identical to the quality it now has; however, I didn't need to speak to anyone in order to pick on their minds Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or to obtain information of -- crucial information through such contact. The purpose of that contact, of the contact that I had with these people was to confirm some of my thoughts, some of the facts that I had arrived at in terms of -- to make it possible for me to draft the report more rapidly. It was not to give others the opportunity of influencing me. I will provide you with an example. My wife would assist me when I needed to refer to certain combat regulations, or when it was necessary for her to bring me books from the library since that is where she works. But I was assisted by her so that I wouldn't have to go to the library every few days. So that I wouldn't have to waste time searching for combat rules or searching for other civilian books that I had to read. My wife assisted me only to help me save time. It has nothing to do with the quality of the report. My wife knows as much about such matters as I do about -- well I don't know, about the cosmos or something else. Status of all the other people that I had contact with was more or less the same as the status of my wife who assisted me by bringing books to me from the library and providing me with the rules and regulations I wanted to consult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to move on to the issue of the questions and the modifications which were brought to the questions. And I refer you to what you said yesterday, and that was on page 49, lines 17 to 25, as well as page 50, lines 1 to 4. Now, this is what you said in response to a question by my colleague. And the question was: "I take it, sir, from this answer, that the questions were amended in such a way so that you could focus your attention and thus reduce the length of your report. Is that a fair overall summary?" And your response was: "Well, roughly speaking, that would be my viewpoint." Now, my question to you is: These questions that were given to you and any modifications thereafter, what was, in your view, the impact of these changes on the drafting of your report, other than, as you say, reducing your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other influence whatsoever. I just needed additional time. Let me give you an example to clarify things. At one point in time, I believe that I was provided with a second group of questions and I believe that there was a subquestion dealing with the communications in the 3rd Corps of the BiH army in the course of 1993. I embarked on answering that question. I prepared grounds for answering that question. I invested some time into answering that question, and later on this question was completely withdrawn. So this would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General, when this question was withdrawn, was it because of the contents of your answer, and had you provided your answer to this question when it was withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this issue of questions, I now refer to page 49, and this is at line 1 to 6, talking about the questions and the corrections. Actually, this is not the right quote. But there is a place where you say, yesterday, about the questions being changed in February. Do you remember saying this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I cannot find the quote, but may I refer you to paragraph 145 in your report. Are you with me on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We discussed already, when I was asking questions last week, as to the fact that the contents of paragraph 145 appeared to be a different version of question number 2. My question to you is whether this is the type of changes that were made, that is between question number 2 in the square that you used and what appears to be the same but in a slightly different manner in paragraph 145. Is this the type of changes that were brought to questions when the question themselves were modified?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now move on to the issue of changes to the report itself. And you mentioned that you were asked to reduce the report and to bring it down, and you mentioned 130 or 150 pages. Now, my question is: Did anyone from the Defence of either General Hadzihasanovic or from the Defence of Brigadier Kubura ever exercise any influence on you with respect to the contents of your report, or the contents of any answers to -- any answer - sorry - to any question in the report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only influence they had was to ask me to reduce the number of pages, if you can consider that influence. And everything else was up to me. So they only had influence on the reduction in the number of pages. There was no other influence whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now of course, General, as I've mentioned yesterday, I take no pleasure in asking these -- sorry, in asking questions like this, because we from the Defence also feel personally involved here, and we don't appreciate it either, but I guess we have to, to fulfil our duty before the Trial Chamber. Now, my next question deals with your reading of the transcript of General Reinhardt. After reading the full transcript of General Reinhardt, how would you qualify his knowledge of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, what do you explain to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my colleague has emphasised the fact that the witness has read the report and he asked him what conclusions he drew from that report. Now I'm asking him about the knowledge that the General Reinhardt had about the situation in Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Mundis, the Defence has asked the expert witness, who had acquainted himself with General Reinhardt's report, what was his opinion of General Reinhardt's information about the war that was taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution's questions were limited to the methodology employed by General Karavelic in producing his report. As part of his answer to one of my questions, he did say that he had read the full transcripts of General Reinhardt's testimony. I did not, however, specifically ask him to comment on any of the conclusions or any of the testimony. And in fact my learned colleague did put questions concerning General Reinhardt's testimony to the witness as part of his direct examination. He could have asked these questions when he conducted his direct examination. I did not specifically ask this witness about the specific contents of General Reinhardt's testimony, nor did I ask him about General Reinhardt's report. Our questions were limited to the methodology, what he did, what he read, et cetera, and we did not get into the merits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. I am going to put the question to the witness. General, you have been asked about your opinion with regard to the fact that another expert drafted a report, and also, in your view, what kind of knowledge could this expert have about the war in your country. Could you please tell us about the knowledge of another expert, about the conflict that had taken place in your country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that General Reinhardt is the person who has achieved a very great military career. In view of all that I know about him, about his training and education from a very young age to the moment when he became a general, he had a lot of training. And throughout his career, he held a number of different positions both in his country, in his own military, as well as in the course of his participation in the international forces at various destinations in Europe and worldwide. As I was reading his report and his transcript, I have to admit that I -- I believe that he approached the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina from a very limited legal and professional aspect. He looked at that situation to a very large extent, and I would find it hard to mention any percentage here, from an angle of a peacetime situation rather than from a wartime situation. In my view, these would be the key objections, if I have any right to voice my objections to that report or parts of General Reinhardt's report. I was not very happy with his overall knowledge of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the course of 1993. I was very happy to find the facts in his report that he looked at from the legal and professional angle and from the angle of a peacetime situation. However, somebody who has held positions in those places as a member of the international forces had to be aware that he was at war and that he was faced with a wartime situation. Whoever knows less about the state of war and about the role and the status, the position and functions of the international forces that were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time and this was similar to other parts of the world and other destinations in the world. However, if I were to compare this - although it is beyond comparison - with the place and role of the international forces in Iraq at the moment and the role and position of international force in Bosnia and Herzegovina for the very reason that the international force in Bosnia-Herzegovina led a life of ease, as if there was peace and that's the way they looked at the war situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And to cut a long story short, I would like to say that I have certain reservations and a certain number of objections, my personal objections to a number of comments for the very reason that he did not look at the situation from the real aspect, and he did not look at the reality of the things that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to move on to a question which was put to you by the Prosecution yesterday and I will read the question. This was at 1800 hours 40 minutes, and the question went as follows: "To the extent you can render your opinion on this as the author of the report, did you take a subjective approach, that is, viewing the events as they happened through the eyes of the two accused, or did you attempt to take an objective approach?" Now, my question to you, General, is, are you familiar with this legal language of objective criteria and subjective criteria in analysing evidence? Are you familiar with these terms?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in response later to -- in the same area when you were questioned by the Prosecution, you responded that what you were trying to do. And this is what you said at 18 hours 42 minutes yesterday, when you said: "I don't know if there's some confusion with regard to the term, but in this paragraph, I wanted to refer to all the events that took place. When I said to look at things through their eyes that means placing myself in their position, in their shoes during that period of time, in order to have the best possible understanding of the situation at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that period of time, during that period of time, and in the belief that that would enable me to be as objective as possible." Now, I stop here and I refer you to your report, and when you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President, just give me a moment. Just bear with me until I find my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I now have it. In response to one of my questions last week, and that was on page 52, lines 16 to 25 and page 53, lines 1 to 11, you said that one issue that stands out -- or rather my question was: "Is there one issue that stands out from your analysis and your drafting of the report?" And you responded that there were two facts, the first one was the concept of reality and the second one was the character of the conflict. Now, my question to you is: When you drafted this paragraph, is this what you had in mind, the concept of reality and the character of the conflict, as you responded last week?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. If I may add to that. My opinion now is that there has been a certain confusion with the use of the term "eyes." I don't know whether I used the term "eyes" in the Bosnian version. Maybe this came out in the English translation, creating this confusion. Everything boils down to the fact that if I were to achieve the highest possible degree of objectivity in representing the reality of the situation, then I would have to place myself in the position of the commander of the 3rd Corps and the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and this is what I did. And I just asked myself how I would have done things under the circumstances, under the influence of all the factors that prevailed in that situation, and of course know that I would have abided by all the rules and regulations, and that was my sole objective. And if I may add to that, in all the militaries of the world, there is one golden rule. When you assess the strength of the enemy, both sides assess their enemy, because they are the two opposing sides. And the rule is always to put yourself in the enemy shoes in order to assess your own strength properly. That was my guiding thought in all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. As a follow-up to this response and to the last two or three questions, I would like to ask whether you agree with the following question and answer which were put to General Sir Martin Garrod, when he testified. And the question was -- and that is on page 8243 of the transcript, the question was: "Now, in this respect, sir, would you agree with me that for anyone to be able to properly assess the work of a commanding officer in an operational situation, this could only be done by taking stock of the prevailing circumstances at the time, and by trying to put one's self, even though that would be very difficult, in the shoes of the commander at the time." And Sir Martin replied: Yes, I think I would agree. Do you agree with the position taken by General Sir Martin Garrod?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time I'm saying what General Garrod said, and I agree with him to the largest extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague yesterday began his cross-examination by asking you to confirm that this was the first time that you acted as an expert witness. And your response was "yes." Do you recall giving this answer?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber provide your opinion whether the fact that this is the first time that you act as an expert witness makes you less of an expert and reduces, in any way, your conclusions in your report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years ago I obtained my Masters degree from the school of political sciences, and a masters degree thesis is a -- is much more than this report. I'm also trying to obtain my doctoral degree, and this will be of great use to me. What I'm trying to say is that this expert report is not something that I had come across before, in terms of its extent and its weight and its demands. I must say that I have done more complex and more elaborate things in my life than this report, and this would be my answer to your question. The truth is, I found myself in the role of an expert for the first time, but this does not have any influence on the quality of my work as an expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If you can just look at the screen in front of you, page 45, line 8, your answer was not interpreted. And the question was: Do you recall answering "yes" to the fact that this was your first time acting as an expert witness. I'm simply asking you, General, to say that the answer that you gave -- I heard you say it, but there were no interpretations. Page 45, line 8. What was your answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
